rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The stones symbolize the lifelessness, powerlessness, and inefficacy of objects worshipped instead of God.
rows.anchor: This evidently denotes all objects of worship to which men turn instead of God - their powerlessness and inefficacy being symbolized by the lifelessness of stones

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Human beings” stands for human actions that deviate from the way of truth.
rows.anchor: the expression "human beings" stands here for human actions deviating from the way of truth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Remembering these objects and actions is bound to intensify the sinner’s suffering in the hereafter, called hell in the Qur’an.
rows.anchor: the remembrance of all of which is bound to increase the sinner's suffering in the hereafter, referred to in the Qur'an as "hell"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Samaʾ means anything spread like a canopy above another thing; it primarily denotes the visible skies in the Qur’an and more broadly a cosmic system.
rows.anchor: anything that is spread like a canopy above any other thing

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In Arabic and apparently other Semitic usage, seven can mean several, while seventy or seven hundred can mean many or very many; Asad cites Lisan al-ʿArab and Taj al-ʿArus.
rows.anchor: in Arabic usage - and apparently in other Semitic languages as well - the number "seven" is often synonymous with "several"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Combining that usage with Raghib’s definition of each heaven relative to what is below it, Asad reads “seven heavens” as multiple cosmic systems.
rows.anchor: every sama' is a sama' with regard to what is below it" (Raghib)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad renders thumma as “and” at the start of this sentence and refers readers to his note on surah 7.
rows.anchor: For my rendering of thumma, at the beginning of this sentence, as "and", see surah 7, first part of note 43.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad renders idh as “lo” here because it can mark a sudden or unexpected event or a turn in discourse, rather than simply “when.”
rows.anchor: idh is also used to indicate "the sudden, or unexpected, occurrence of a thing" (cf. Lane 1, 39), or a sudden turn in the discourse

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ensuing allegory about reason implanted in human beings connects logically with the preceding passages.
rows.anchor: The subsequent allegory, relating as it does to the faculty of reason implanted in man, is logically connected with the preceding passages.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khalifah derives from khalafa, “he succeeded”; in this allegory it denotes humanity’s rightful supremacy on earth, which Asad renders as inheriting the earth.
rows.anchor: used in this allegory to denote man's rightful supremacy on earth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad connects this reading to verses that call human beings khalaʾif al-arḍ, successors on earth.
rows.anchor: where all human beings are - spoken of as khala'if al-ard

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an does not specify the form of the punishment; lexicographers differ on the word’s interpretation but agree it conveys vehemence and suddenness.
rows.anchor: The lexicographers give various interpretations to this word, but all agree on the element of vehemence and suddenness inherent in it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad reads the passage as establishing that the Qur’anic dispensation supersedes the earlier Biblical dispensation.
rows.anchor: relating to the supersession of the Biblical dispensation by that of the Qur'an

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In this context ayah means “message”; its use elsewhere for a Qur’anic verse led some theologians to an erroneous doctrine of internal Qur’anic abrogation, which Asad rejects.
rows.anchor: by many Muslim theologians. The word ayah ("message") occurring in this, context is also used to denote a "verse;" of the Qur'an

rows.speaker: many Muslim theologians
rows.claim: They take ayah to mean a Qur’anic verse and conclude that some verses were abrogated before revelation ended; Asad calls this assertion fanciful.
rows.anchor: by many Muslim theologians. The word ayah ("message") occurring in this, context is also used to denote a "verse;" of the Qur'an

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad likens the claim that Qur’anic verses were revised during revelation to imagining a human author editing manuscript proofs after the fact.
rows.anchor: the image of a human author correcting, on second thought, the proofs of his manuscript - deleting one passage and replacing it with another

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad says no reliable Tradition reports that the Prophet ever declared a Qur’anic verse abrogated, undermining the doctrine’s historical basis.
rows.anchor: there does not exist a single reliable Tradition to the effect that the Prophet ever, declared a verse of the Qur'an to have been "abrogated"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad traces the doctrine to early commentators’ inability to reconcile Qur’anic passages, which they resolved by declaring one abrogated.
rows.anchor: the inability of some of the early commentators to reconcile one Qur'anic passage with another

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This arbitrary method explains the lack of agreement on which or how many verses were affected and whether abrogation removed a verse entirely or canceled only its ruling or statement.
rows.anchor: why there is no unanimity whatsoever among the upholders of the "doctrine of abrogation" as to which, and how many, Qur'an verses have been affected by it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Read with 2:105, which says Jews and Christians reject revelation superseding the Bible, the verse concerns earlier divine messages, not parts of the Qur’an.
rows.anchor: if read in this way, the abrogation relates to the earlier divine messages and not to any part of the Qur'an itself

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad notes that the phrase translated “from among them” literally means “within them.”
rows.anchor: Lit., "within them".

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khayr here means “much wealth,” not merely property; sayings of A’ishah and Ali ibn Abi Talib support this reading, as do Zamakhshari and Baydawi.
rows.anchor: The word khayr occurring in this sentence denotes "much wealth" and not simply "property"

rows.speaker: A'ishah and Ali ibn Abi Talib
rows.claim: Sayings of A’ishah and Ali ibn Abi Talib, both referring to this verse, support reading khayr as much wealth.
rows.anchor: supported by sayings of 'A'ishah and 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, both of them referring to this particular verse

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those leaving much wealth should bequeath to particularly deserving family members in addition to, and before distributing, the fixed inheritance shares in 4:11–12.
rows.anchor: make bequests to particularly deserving members of his family in addition to - and preceding the distribution of - the legally - fixed shares mentioned in 4:11-12

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase literally means “witnesses” or “is present in,” explaining Asad’s rendering “lives to see” the month.
rows.anchor: Lit., "witnesses" or "is present in".

rows.speaker: Most of the commentators
rows.claim: Most commentators take the comparison to fathers as referring to pre-Islamic Arabs’ custom of praising their ancestors’ greatness and supposed virtues at gatherings.
rows.anchor: Most of the commentators see in this passage a reference to the custom of the pre-Islamic Arabs to extol

rows.speaker: Ad-Dahhak, Ar-Rabi and Abu Muslim
rows.claim: These early scholars instead understand the words as referring to actual fathers or, by implication, both parents, whom children regard as embodiments of goodness and power.
rows.anchor: e.g., Ad-Dahhak, Ar-Rabi and Abu Muslim - are of the opinion that what is meant here are actual fathers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ithm literally means sin or anything conducive to sinning; because it is contrasted with benefits, Asad considers “evil” a suitable rendering.
rows.anchor: Lit., "sin", or anything that is conducive to sinning.

rows.speaker: Razi
rows.claim: Razi and other classical commentators point out that ithm is used as the antithesis of manafiʿ, “benefits.”
rows.anchor: As some of the classical commentators (e.g., Razi) point out, the term ithm is used in this verse as the antithesis of manafi' ("benefits")

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although this verse says their evil outweighs their benefit, Asad points to the clear prohibition of intoxicants and games of chance in 5:90–91.
rows.anchor: For a clear-cut prohibition of intoxicants and games of chance, see 5:90-91 and the corresponding notes.

rows.speaker: Muhammad 'Abduh
rows.claim: Muhammad Abduh explains the wrong as deliberately turning away from the light of God’s guidance.
rows.anchor: According to Muhammad 'Abduh, the wrong (zulm) referred to here consists in "one's deliberately turning away

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reading treats the following passage through 3:51 as part of the angel’s announcement to Mary, implying Jesus would say these words in the future.
rows.anchor: as part of the announcement made to Mary (implying that he would thus speak in the future)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad prefers reading it as what Jesus later said to the children of Israel, since the narrative from 3:52 onward supports that reading.
rows.anchor: as a statement of what, at a later time, he actually did say to the children of Israel

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad’s reason for preferring the later speech reading is the narrative form adopted from verse 52 onward.
rows.anchor: In view of the narrative form adopted in verses 52 ff., the second of these two alternatives seems preferable.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tayr can be a plural of ta’ir, “flying creature” or “bird,” or an infinitive meaning “flying” from tara, “he flew.”
rows.anchor: The noun tayr is a plural of ta'ir ("flying creature" or "bird"), or an infinitive noun ("flying")

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In pre-Islamic usage and the Qur’an, ta’ir and tayr often mean fortune or destiny, good or evil; Asad cites 7:131, 27:47, 36:19, and 17:13 and dictionaries including Lane.
rows.anchor: words ta'ir and tayr often denote "fortune" or "destiny", whether good or evil

words: أَخْلُقُ لَكُم مِّنَ ٱلطِّينِ كَهَيْـَٔةِ ٱلطَّيْرِ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad reads Jesus’ parable as fashioning a soaring vision of destiny from the humble clay of people’s lives, made real through God-given inspiration, God’s leave, and faith.
rows.anchor: out of the humble clay of their lives he would fashion for them the vision of a soaring destiny

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad considers it probable that Jesus’ raising the dead metaphorically means giving new life to people spiritually dead, as in 6:122.
rows.anchor: giving new life to people who were spiritually dead

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the raising of the dead is metaphorical, healing the blind and lepers similarly means inner regeneration of people spiritually diseased and blind to truth.
rows.anchor: the "healing of the blind and the leper" has a similar significance: namely, an inner regeneration

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The things people eat are good things enjoyed in this life, while what they store up means good deeds laid up for the life to come.
rows.anchor: what good things you may partake of in the life of this world, and what good deeds you should lay up as a treasure for the life to come

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word shay’an makes shirk broader than worshipping other deities: it includes assigning divine or quasi-divine powers to people or objects not viewed as deities, such as saint-worship.
rows.anchor: is not confined to a worship of other "deities", but implies also the attribution of divine or quasi-divine powers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Your own people” means someone from your own community, not an actual relative, since near of kin were already mentioned; the other neighbor is from another community.
rows.anchor: the expression "your own people" (dhu l-qurba) refers to the community and not to one's actual relatives

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet stressed believers’ moral duty to neighbors regardless of faith, summarized by the instruction to do good to one’s neighbor; Asad cites Bukhari, Muslim, and other compilations.
rows.anchor: The Prophet often stressed a believer's moral obligation towards his neighbours, whatever their faith
